title: CAST: Real-Time Motion Capture for Any Skeleton Topology
shortTitle: CAST: Real-Time Motion Capture for Any Skeleton Topology
abstract: This paper studies the problem of recovering motion from monocular video, even when the target skeleton topology differs from the subject observed in the video. Although previous methods have made efforts to resolve this problem, they remain vulnerable to joint-rotation errors that are coupled across the skeleton and can propagate along its kinematic hierarchy. To mitigate these errors, we present CAST, a topology-aware motion capture framework that combines learned local rotations with geometric correction guided by predicted global bone directions. Our observability analysis characterizes which rotational components can be constrained by outgoing bone directions. Guided by this analysis, GRACE uses reliability-gated alignment to correct composed orientations in parent-to-child order, leaving unconstrained components to the learned rotation predictor. The motion predictor and correction module are trained jointly with motion-derived supervision, using a frozen image encoder. Experiments under the TopoCap evaluation protocol show that the proposed framework improves motion recovery across different target topologies, including unseen structures. Reference-based cross-skeleton evaluation on a curated Mixamo benchmark and a user preference study further assess transfer to different target structures. A causal CAST-B variant achieves over 51 FPS on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, with timing covering image encoding and motion prediction. Code repository: https://github.com/fankewen/CAST.

title: Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds
shortTitle: Terrarium: Growing Personal Assistants via Scalable Synthesis of App Worlds
abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought the vision of a general-purpose personal assistant closer to reality. Such assistants could provide a unified natural-language interface to a broad ecosystem of applications. However, real-world applications do not readily support training at scale because access is often restricted and their state is difficult to reset. To address this challenge, we introduce Terrarium, a framework that synthesizes executable App Worlds from real-world application information, generates training task packages with evaluator-side rubrics from these worlds, and iteratively validates and refines both through agent rollouts. For App World synthesis, Terrarium organizes public Web information and in-application observations into structured app specifications that guide the construction of self-contained runtimes with callable operations and mutable, resettable state. For task synthesis, Terrarium constructs tasks grounded in App World state together with evaluator-side outcome rubrics that assess success without prescribing reference trajectories. We construct a training suite of 275 App Worlds and 13,344 tasks for outcome-based reinforcement learning across three Qwen3 model scales (4B, 8B, and 14B parameters). Across these scales, models trained with Terrarium outperform the corresponding Qwen3 models by an average of 18.34 percentage points on the $τ^2$-bench and 10.94 percentage points on the AppWorld bench. These results suggest that app-grounded world and task synthesis offers a scalable path toward general-purpose assistants capable of operating across broad application ecosystems.

title: World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting
shortTitle: World2TS: Real-World Event Context for Time-Series Forecasting
abstract: Time-series forecasting plays a vital role in a wide range of real-world applications. Recent approaches have achieved strong performance by modeling temporal correlations and cross-channel dependencies, yet most forecasting benchmarks still represent time series primarily as numerical histories. In practice, time series are observations of complex real-world processes, and their trajectories may reflect events, interventions, disruptions, and changes in measurement or reporting that cannot always be inferred from past values alone. A central barrier to studying context-aware forecasting is therefore the lack of large-scale datasets that align real-world events with the individual series they affect. We present World2TS, a scalable construction framework and large-scale dataset for time-series forecasting with real-world event context. We first develop world2ts-core, a reusable tool that combines agent-led semantic reasoning and Web search, command-line execution and validation, and human review within a feedback-driven discovery workflow. Given heterogeneous time series with semantic descriptions, the workflow discovers candidate events, consolidates retrieved evidence into verified events, and links them to relevant series under explicit temporal and semantic scopes. Using this framework, we construct world2ts-data, which contains 31 datasets across six domains, comprising 4,179 series, 97.1 million observations, 1,159 events, and 56,846 event-series links. We further conduct extensive data analyses and controlled comparative experiments to characterize the dataset and demonstrate the utility of the collected context for improving forecasting accuracy. World2TS provides a reusable data foundation for developing and evaluating context-aware forecasting models and agents. The project homepage is available at https://world2ts.github.io/.

title: Blending experimental electron density information to protein-ligand interaction
shortTitle: Blending experimental electron density information to protein-ligand interaction
abstract: Machine learning models for protein-ligand interactions commonly rely on atomic coordinates, which are constructed by fitting molecular models to experimental electron-density maps. However, most models represent each complex as a single fitted structure, which can omit information about conformational heterogeneity, positional uncertainty, and local density support for individual atoms at binding interfaces. To fill this gap, we present CoDE, a Coordinate and Density Encoder, pre-trained on experimental density maps. We represent each binding site on a shared three-dimensional voxel grid combining atomic occupancy, experimental electron density, and its gradient magnitude. Using approximately 100K curated complexes, we pre-train a channel-wise vision transformer to jointly reconstruct masked atomic and density channels, learning a representation that integrates structural and experimental information. We evaluate the frozen encoder on two downstream tasks: (i) binding-affinity regression under leakage-controlled splits and (ii) pocket-conditioned ligand generation. Across these settings, CoDE improves over an identically pre-trained coordinate-only encoder and remains competitive with task-specific baselines, showing that density complements fitted atomic coordinates for protein-ligand interaction modeling and that the density-blended representation is useful for structure-based ligand generation.

title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
shortTitle: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. We evaluate WeatherBridge using daily GFS, HRES, and CMA initializations from 1 January to 22 November 2025 across six variables and lead times up to 240 hours. Relative to raw source initialization of FuXi, WeatherBridge reduces the mean RMSE of FuXi over the 6- 240-hour rollout for 17 of 18 source-variable combinations, with a median reduction of 10.2% and a maximum reduction of 46.3%. The adapter trained with frozen FuXi also improves FengWu forecasts on GFS inputs without retraining either the adapter or FengWu. These results demonstrate that forecast-aware input adaptation can improve forecasts from heterogeneous operational NWP inputs and transfer across pretrained ERA5-based forecasting models.

title: Predict in Chunks, Revise in Spans: History-conditioned Action Regeneration for Robotic Manipulation
shortTitle: Predict in Chunks, Revise in Spans: History-conditioned Action Regeneration for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.

title: ScalLoc: Continuous Oblique Thermal UAV Geo-Localization with a 2D Satellite Map
shortTitle: ScalLoc: Continuous Oblique Thermal UAV Geo-Localization with a 2D Satellite Map
abstract: Cross-modal Thermal Geo-localization (TG) provides an illumination-robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied environments. However, existing thermal geo-localization methods mainly focus on near-nadir observations or depend on map-side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo-referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale-aligned local-to-map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo-localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction--refinement--anchoring--propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track-based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame-level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal-Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day--night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame-level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT-only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame-weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo-localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
shortTitle: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. We propose ***MORE***, a V-JEPA framework that learns **M**otion-**O**riented **RE**gisters during video pretraining as a shared state interface for driving world models and planning. MORE injects temporally aligned ego motion into a small set of registers and uses them as the sole context for masked patch prediction, channeling dense patch-level supervision through a compact state bottleneck. A complementary blockwise register-masking objective further shapes predictive structure in the register space. During downstream training, the same register space defines the future states predicted by the world model and provides shared scene memory for trajectory generation and scoring. On NAVSIM-v2, MORE outperforms the state of the art by 1.6 in EPDMS, while achieving superior efficiency with only 1/10 the inference latency of DriveLaW. These results support learning the state interface for world modeling and planning directly during video pretraining.

title: Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction
shortTitle: Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction
abstract: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

title: Contrastive Linearized Laplace: Loss Geometry, Valid Repairs, and Reliable Cores
shortTitle: Contrastive Linearized Laplace: Loss Geometry, Valid Repairs, and Reliable Cores
abstract: While contrastive learning is widely used to learn deterministic representations, it does not inherently provide estimates of uncertainty. Post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods, such as the Linearized Laplace approximation (LLA), offer a way to quantify uncertainty without retraining the encoder. However, we show that directly using the LLA induced distribution over the contrastive embedding does not yield reliable pointwise uncertainty estimates for downstream tasks: embedding variance alone does not reflect whether decisions such as nearest-neighbor retrieval or cluster assignment are stable. To address this limitation, we develop a post-hoc framework based on LLA that propagates encoder uncertainty through the downstream task. We characterize the curvature of contrastive objectives and introduce positive-semidefinite repairs where needed to obtain valid local Gaussian approximations without retraining the encoder. We test the proposed approach in metagenomic binning and image classification tasks. For metagenomic binning, posterior coassignment probabilities support consensus partitions and the selection of reliable cores, leading to improvements over existing baselines. Additional image classification experiments show calibration improvements on standard benchmarks and real histopathology datasets.

title: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
shortTitle: Beyond Outcome Feedback: Trajectory-Quality-Guided Experience-based Learning
abstract: Experience-based learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to improve over time by reusing knowledge from past executions. However, existing methods typically rely on final task outcomes as feedback for experience learning, overlooking the execution process and limiting their ability to evaluate and optimize experience based on trajectory quality. To address this limitation, we propose TQG-Exp, a trajectory-quality-guided experience-based learning framework that introduces process feedback. Specifically, we introduce Trajectory Quality Loss (TQL), which jointly considers task completion and process quality to provide a learning signal beyond final task outcomes. Based on this signal, we employ paired rollouts with and without retrieved experience to guide experience optimization. Representative trajectories are selected based on their outcomes and trajectory quality to extract task-level and task-type-level experiences. Meanwhile, differences in trajectory quality between the paired groups are used to estimate the contribution of retrieved experience and update its utility. The learned utility is then combined with semantic relevance to guide subsequent experience retrieval. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld with two backbone LLMs show that TQG-Exp outperforms existing experience-based methods, improving Avg.@3 over the strongest baseline by 4.50 and 8.55 percentage points on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.5-Flash, respectively.

title: Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions
shortTitle: Social Bias in Chinese Large Language Models under Social Media Expressions
abstract: Existing Chinese social-bias benchmarks for large language models largely rely on normalized or template-based expressions, leaving the influence of internet slang, emoji, and sarcasm insufficiently examined. Safety alignment may further compress conventional plausibility ratings toward the lower end of the scale. This study constructs 73 paired probes across gender, region, and occupation. Each probe contains a neutral expression, a social-media-style expression, and a reversed-identity control. The task is reframed from direct plausibility judgment to social consensus estimation. Social-media expressions are divided into stylistic packaging, which preserves semantic polarity, and sarcastic packaging, which reverses surface polarity. Six Chinese-capable large language models are evaluated through paired differences measuring identity bias, stylistic packaging, and sarcasm shift. All models show significant identity-bias effects; five show significantly negative stylistic-packaging effects; and sarcasm shifts display a clear cross-model gradient. These findings demonstrate that expression form is not a transparent carrier in bias evaluation and that lower scores under sarcasm should not be interpreted directly as bias mitigation. The proposed paired design offers a measurement approach for Chinese social-media contexts while also revealing the construct boundary and prompt sensitivity of social consensus estimation.

title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
shortTitle: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.

title: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
shortTitle: Verify, Act, Distill: Turning Test-Time Compute into Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.

title: Agent-Guided Evidence Acquisition for Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction
shortTitle: Agent-Guided Evidence Acquisition for Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction
abstract: Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction (ECPE) requires identifying the causes associated with emotions expressed in a conversation. Accurate extraction can depend on evidence that is not initially available, making it important to decide when further information is worth acquiring. We study agent-guided evidence acquisition for ECPE, where a student agent selectively accesses expert judgments for borderline relations on both sides of its validation-selected F1 decision boundary and revises only queried predictions. Through controlled comparisons under different information-access conditions, we examine how delegation granularity, query selection, and response integration affect prediction quality. At a nominal 10% query rate, selective fusion improves mean pair F1 by 2.64-3.88 points over the student in our main experiments, reaching 65.14 on ECF and 49.74 on MEC4 across model families. Our analysis suggests that greater access does not always translate into better cause identification. These findings motivate acquisition strategies that consider both the relevance of newly available evidence and its effect on prediction revision, providing an empirical basis for more effective and efficient evidence acquisition in ECPE.

title: LETS: Low-Overhead External-Torque Sensing for Force-Feedback Bilateral Teleoperation
shortTitle: LETS: Low-Overhead External-Torque Sensing for Force-Feedback Bilateral Teleoperation
abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.

title: Description Complexity Bounds for Analytic Approximations of Lipschitz Functions
shortTitle: Description Complexity Bounds for Analytic Approximations of Lipschitz Functions
abstract: We study how many bits are needed to write down an elementary analytic expression that uniformly approximates a Lipschitz function. Expressions are finite trees over the basis $\{+,-,\times,÷,\exp\}$ with the variables and rational constants, and their size is $\dc(f)$, the length of the shortest description of $f$ in a fixed binary description language. For functions of one variable we prove that every $L$-Lipschitz $F:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ has an everywhere-defined approximant of accuracy $Δ$ with $\dc(f)\le C\,(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$ for all $L,Δ>0$, by a linear spline smoothed with logistic ramps in a description language with one repetition construct. We prove a matching lower bound valid for \emph{every} description language: for $Δ\le 1/36$ and every $L>0$ some $L$-Lipschitz function needs at least $\tfrac1{16}(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$ bits. Hence the worst-case description complexity is $Θ(L/Δ+\lg(1/Δ+2))$. For functions on $[0,1]^d$ the same method gives $Θ_d\bigl((L/Δ)^d+\lg(1/Δ+2)\bigr)$, using a tensor-product spline whose coefficients are mixed second differences and cost $O(d)$ bits each. Without the repetition construct the upper bounds carry an additional logarithmic factor, whose necessity for plain expression trees is left open. A reference encoder, decoder and evaluator confirm the constructions numerically, and figures and tables report the checks.

title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
shortTitle: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
abstract: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.

title: Test-Time Compute for Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models
shortTitle: Test-Time Compute for Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models
abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.

title: TeachGrade: Training-Free Short Answer Scoring with Teacher Evidence
shortTitle: TeachGrade: Training-Free Short Answer Scoring with Teacher Evidence
abstract: Multi-subject, multi-step scoring requires consistent partial credit across grading conventions. We introduce TeachGrade, a training-free framework using teacher-graded examples. The Task Adapt module builds two frozen memories: Skill captures contextual teacher preferences beyond the rubric; CaseBank supplies local evidence. PreJudge provides retrieval cues; FinalJudge regrades the answer without preliminary scores. On 3,829 SAS-Bench answers across 12 tasks, official macro collaborative consistency score (CCS) rises from Native's 67.99 to 81.32 (+13.33 points), and pooled step exact match from 54.85% to 62.71%. Macro quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) reaches 84.71, exceeding Native, OpenJudge, ProofGrader, and Trojsten by 9.52, 3.50, 11.37, and 17.43 points, respectively, and leading on 8 tasks. Local Qwen3.8-27B gains 8.83 CCS and 4.08 QWK points, improving CCS on all 12 tasks. QWK gains over Native span 6.38--14.65 points on Portuguese automatic essay scoring (AES) and 2.16--2.24 on ASAP-SAS across label views, with lower mean absolute error. These results support reuse across languages, response formats, and backbones without weight updates.

title: Conflict-Aware Autonomous Resource Orchestration for 5G Edge Slicing Using Multi-Agent Systems and LLMs
shortTitle: Conflict-Aware Autonomous Resource Orchestration for 5G Edge Slicing Using Multi-Agent Systems and LLMs
abstract: 5G edge network slicing must reconcile two coupled requirements: understanding high-level operator intent and reallocating scarce computing and bandwidth resources under dynamic contention. Centralized optimization can face computational and responsiveness challenges under rapidly changing edge contention, and Multi-Agent System (MAS)-based auctions can support resource arbitration but still depend on operator-defined economic parameters and priorities. Embedding a Large Language Model (LLM) directly in a recurring control loop, by contrast, may introduce non-negligible inference latency and non-deterministic behavior. This paper proposes a two-timescale architecture that addresses this gap: an LLM-based Strategist translates natural-language network intents into economic policy parameters (budget, income, and bidding-aggressiveness) at the macro scale, while a deterministic, Vickrey-inspired second-price mechanism run by SPADE-based slice agents resolves recurring resource contention at the operational scale, with the resulting allocations enforced by patching Kubernetes CPU limits and Calico CNI bandwidth annotations directly on User Plane Function pods. We evaluate the architecture end-to-end on a real Kubernetes/Open5GS edge cluster across two complementary scenarios, each repeated 30 times: a Smart-City scenario, in which natural-language public-safety intents propagate into measurable changes in slice bids and bandwidth allocations within a few auction rounds, and a Hierarchical-slicing scenario, in which the mechanism provides priority-dependent resource and QoE differentiation, adapts to abrupt demand changes, and preserves configured minimum guarantees while maintaining near-complete allocation of the shared bandwidth pool.

title: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
shortTitle: Scalable Multi-Human Cooperative Manipulation via Commander-Executor Coordination
abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.

title: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
shortTitle: Probable but Not Valid: A Psychometric Audit of Decision Models as Synthetic Survey Respondents
abstract: Language models are increasingly used to create synthetic survey samples, also called silicon samples. Decision models are a new class of language models that return a probability for each point of a rating scale instead of text. We ask whether these models, or the newest generative LLMs, can stand in for human respondents on a psychometric survey. We test fourteen decision models from eleven providers and 47 generative LLMs on an open Lithuanian organisational-psychology survey (n=263, 68 items), with 100 real respondent profiles, the Psychometric Similarity Score (PSS) and statistical baselines. The best generative model, MiniMax M3, reaches PSS 0.813. This is level with a Gaussian copula fit only on other respondents (0.824) and below a copula fit in sample (0.927). A second sample of 100 real people scores below the best models, so at this size PSS cannot rank them against real respondents. In 5 of 10 product lines the newest generative release scores below an earlier release of the same line beyond resampling noise, and none gains beyond it. With the default rounded readout, 13 of 14 decision models score below the generative reference gpt-5.4-mini. Of the 47 generative models, 33 reproduce the pattern of item correlations better than any decision model. Averaged over respondents, the probability vectors are much closer to the human item marginals than rounded answers. They also rank respondents about as well as a profile regression fit on 163 real people. As forecasts of each person's own answers, however, every decision model is worse than the answer frequencies of other respondents, mainly because its average vector differs from them. The profile regression improves on these frequencies by only 1.0%, so the profile fields say little about how a person answers. Synthetic respondents built on such profiles should therefore aim at sample-level fidelity.

title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
shortTitle: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

title: WorkBorne: Discovering Agentic Tasks from Real-World Artifact Transitions
shortTitle: WorkBorne: Discovering Agentic Tasks from Real-World Artifact Transitions
abstract: Developing terminal-based agents for long-horizon execution demands synthetic tasks that tightly couple complex instructions with authentic, interactive environments. However, current automated synthesis suffers from a fundamental asymmetry: instruction-oriented methods fabricate low-fidelity, synthetic environments, whereas resource-oriented methods treat real artifacts merely as static inputs, degrading task instructions into shallow, trivial operations. To address this limitation, we introduce WorkBorne, a synthesis framework that uses artifact transitions as the central primitive for modeling the full life-cycle of agentic tasks. In WorkBorne, each transition specifies who performs the task, which artifacts anchor the initial state and intended outcome, and the corresponding relationship between them. Specifically, WorkBorne first constructs coherent and diverse artifact corpora from iterative web retrieval, then discovers non-trivial transitions by identifying meaningful input-output artifact assemblies and the relations that connect them. Each discovered transition is finally instantiated into grounded agentic tasks. We construct 1,061 artifact corpora and 7,882 task environments, yielding 15,485 high-quality trajectories, with 53.6% exceeding 30 assistant turns. Experiments on Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B show that WorkBorne substantially improves over base models (i.e., improving Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 43.1% to 61.8% and ClawEval General score from 75.0 to 80.2) and achieves the strongest overall performance among other synthesis baselines (e.g., TMax (Ivison et al., 2026), RST (Li et al., 2026a), Terminal-Universe (Wu et al., 2026a)). Further analysis shows that transition is strongly associated with execution depth, while corpus breadth and transition depth provide complementary scaling gains.

title: Funnel planning and control for manipulators using neural Signed Configuration Distance Functions
shortTitle: Funnel planning and control for manipulators using neural Signed Configuration Distance Functions
abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.

title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
shortTitle: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications
abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $Δ19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $Δ5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.

title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
shortTitle: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.

title: Edge-Native Temporal--Graph Dual-Expert Inference for Dexterous Grasp Classification
shortTitle: Edge-Native Temporal--Graph Dual-Expert Inference for Dexterous Grasp Classification
abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.

title: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
shortTitle: FidelityQ: Preserving Predictive Fidelity in Ultra-Low-Bit Language Model Quantization
abstract: Ultra-low-bit scalar quantization offers a regular arithmetic structure for efficient deployment of large language models, but preserving predictive behavior at extreme precision remains challenging: with only a few reconstruction levels, accurate weight representation must translate into consistent predictions from a small calibration set. We propose FidelityQ, a scalar quantization framework that preserves predictive fidelity at weight precisions down to 2 bits. For accurate quantization, we introduce Information-Aligned Analytic Coding (IAC), which shapes each weight row toward a centered symmetric source via randomized Hadamard mixing and fits a mirrored four-level minimum-distortion quantizer to its empirical weights. Every level set in this family decomposes exactly into two sign-valued bases with associated scales, combining source-adaptive reconstruction with lookup-free decoding compatible with scaled integer arithmetic. Our analysis further shows that residual predictive discrepancies are heavy-tailed and concentrate on tokens the teacher predicts confidently, motivating Knowledge-Intensive Calibration (KIC) for consistent quantization. KIC ranks sequences by the tail of token-wise teacher-student divergence, allocates a limited calibration budget to the highest-scoring samples, and restores predictive agreement by updating only quantization levels and scales under teacher supervision, keeping pretrained weights frozen. Experiments on the LLaMA and Qwen families demonstrate the effectiveness of FidelityQ in weight-only and joint quantization settings. On LLaMA-2-7B, FidelityQ achieves a WikiText2 perplexity of 6.62 at W2A16 and improves the prior state-of-the-art W2A4KV4 result from 8.31 to 6.96, while reducing linear-layer weight memory by 8.0x relative to FP16.

title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
shortTitle: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.

title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
shortTitle: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.

title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
shortTitle: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
abstract: How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles. Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model. When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.

title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
shortTitle: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.

title: Engram Neuron Inspired Adaptive Memorization for Lifelong Learning
shortTitle: Engram Neuron Inspired Adaptive Memorization for Lifelong Learning
abstract: Lifelong learning enables artificial systems to adapt to changing environments. To achieve this, an effective artificial learner should dynamically reorganize past and new experiences, maintaining stability while enabling flexible knowledge integration. However, existing efforts primarily mitigate catastrophic forgetting, lacking the ability to adaptively update memory akin to biological systems. Here, by integrating the full memory life cycle of engram neurons into artificial learners, we propose a framework that constructs a structured memory from gradient representations, which regulates parameter updates and guides memory management. Through comprehensive evaluations on four benchmarks, our approach shows promising lifelong learning capability, maintaining stability over long task sequences and supporting flexible adaptation. Beyond the performance gains, our approach offers a computational perspective on robust and flexible lifelong learning, echoing mechanisms observed in biological memory systems.

title: Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: Compositional Average Velocity Modeling for Efficient Diffusion Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Source Data Selection via Learnable Categorical Priors: Variance Reduction and Guaranteed Derandomization
shortTitle: Probabilistic Multi-Source Data Selection via Learnable Categorical Priors: Variance Reduction and Guaranteed Derandomization
abstract: Bilevel data selection is a fundamental task with numerous applications in machine learning and statistics. A common strategy for tackling this problem is to relax the original bilevel combinatorial optimization into a continuous one. However, existing methods, including 0-1 relaxation and probabilistic relaxation, still suffer from several limitations, such as unstable gradient estimation and infeasible rounding. To address these issues, this paper proposes a new probabilistic relaxation for the multi-source bilevel data selection problem. Our key idea is to introduce multiple learnable categorical priors to parameterize a probability distribution supported only on feasible data subsets, thus naturally yielding a lossless rounding scheme. We further show that our proposed relaxation admits an effective two-point gradient estimator, which can simultaneously avoid the inverse-Hessian computation required by existing 0-1 relaxation and the unbounded score term appearing in prior probabilistic relaxation. Furthermore, we develop a reducible representation of this estimator, which substantially reduces the number of lower-level retrainings required for gradient computation. Built upon this reducible two-point estimator, we then design a novel stochastic gradient algorithm, termed ReSGD, for multi-source bilevel data selection problem, and establish a rigorous approximation guarantee for the subset returned by ReSGD under weak submodularity. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed ReSGD.

title: Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation via Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations
shortTitle: Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation via Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations
abstract: Specifying segmentation targets with natural language provides flexible semantic conditioning for medical image segmentation. However, existing methods still struggle to reliably ground high-level textual semantics into accurate pixel-level spatial prompts, especially under low-contrast lesions, ambiguous boundaries, and visually similar anatomical contexts. In this paper, we propose RADAR (Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations), a parameter-efficient framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. RADAR explicitly decouples and synergizes the medical semantic anchoring capability of BiomedCLIP with the prompt-driven mask decoding ability of MedSAM2, while enabling low-cost task adaptation via LoRA. Specifically, Guided Residual Depth Aggregation adaptively aggregates cross-layer features under semantic guidance to alleviate delayed textual injection and deep semantic dilution. Structured Dense Representation Alignment leverages a frozen BiomedCLIP to construct crop-level target, boundary, and context anchors, improving the local discriminability of dense features and the reliability of automatic prompts. Multi-modal Prompt Generation further converts cross-modal semantic responses into composite text, point, and mask prompts for MedSAM2 decoding. Experiments on three public medical image segmentation datasets show that RADAR achieves competitive performance with only 0.74M trainable parameters, demonstrating its effectiveness in parameter-efficient adaptation, semantic grounding, and dense representation enhancement. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/RADAR.

title: DSM-Free UAV Visual Localization via Latent-Depth Variable Projection and Structure-Adaptive Coupling
shortTitle: DSM-Free UAV Visual Localization via Latent-Depth Variable Projection and Structure-Adaptive Coupling
abstract: Visual localization enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to maintain absolute positioning in GNSS-denied environments. A common approach matches UAV images with geo-tagged orthographic maps and estimates camera pose using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) with elevations from Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, accurate and up-to-date DSMs are often unavailable in practice. Orthographic-perspective geometry (OPG) enables DSM-free localization in scenes with varying elevations, yet existing methods typically estimate pose indirectly through intermediate matrix estimation and decomposition. To address this limitation, we propose Latent-Depth Variable Projection (LDVP), which treats the unknown scales along perspective viewing rays as latent depths. By analytically eliminating these depths and solving for the horizontal camera center in closed form given the rotation, LDVP reduces nonlinear estimation to a rotation-only problem, enabling direct recovery of metric horizontal position without assuming a planar scene. To improve localization robustness across different scene structures, we further introduce Structure-Adaptive Coupling (SAC), which uses relative scene structure inferred from monocular depth estimation to select LDVP when the matched points are not dominated by a single plane, and Planar-PnP otherwise. Our local observability analysis reveals how scene elevation variation affects the geometric constraints of OPG, providing a basis for this adaptive strategy. Extensive experiments show that LDVP consistently outperforms existing OPG-based DSM-free methods, while SAC further improves robustness across diverse scenes and substantially narrows the gap to DSM-based localization. Code will be released at https://github.com/UAV-AVL/LDVP-SAC.

title: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
shortTitle: FoundationVIO: Enforcing Metric Scale in Feed-forward Visual-Inertial Odometry
abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models (GFMs) directly predict dense geometry and camera poses from batches of images. Emerging visual SLAM methods chain together consecutive GFM batches to form dense point cloud maps. A core challenge is how to address the ambiguous geometric scale of GFM predictions: independent predictions are locally consistent up-to-scale but not constrained by any direct physical measurements. Models trained on data with known scale improve the consistency of GFM reconstructions but again do not directly measure it. Consequently, trajectories and 3D reconstructions from GFM-enabled SLAM methods inherit this issue. Motivated by parallels with classical visual-inertial odometry, we introduce FoundationVIO which integrates inertial sensing with GFM predictions to recover metric scale reconstruction using a factor-graph based approach. We demonstrate odometry estimates competitive with classical state-of-the-art VIO methods and accurate dense reconstructions that outperform GFM-enabled SLAM methods. We also add a minimal GFM-based loop-closure mechanism to create a full Visual-Inertial SLAM system capable of creating globally accurate reconstructions and pose estimates. We evaluate our method on three datasets with well known sensor systems and demonstrate its compatibility on ubiquitous camera and IMU sensors. The method runs at approximately real-time on a consumer-grade laptop GPU. Code: https://github.com/ori-drs/FoundationVIO.

title: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
shortTitle: Do Personalized LLMs Need the Whole Conversation? Matching the Full History with Only 5% of Its Text via Relevance-Filtered Context
abstract: Personalized assistants accumulate long conversation histories, and passing the whole history to an LLM with every request is costly. We show that it is also unnecessary. On PersonaMem-v2 (180 questions), with GPT-5.6-terra and Claude Opus 5.5 as judges, a relevance-filtered context, built by sentence-level retrieval that ranks the history by similarity to the current request and stops at a fixed budget, matches full-history accuracy with only 5% of the text, cutting the judge's input about 20-fold. An LLM summary of the same length performs on par, but it needs an LLM to read the entire history, whereas retrieval needs only a small embedding model. While both sentence-level retrieval and LLM summary perform strongly, retrieval does so while placing the relevant evidence in the context for only 61% of the questions, and an oracle given only that evidence beats the full history by 15.6 points, making better context selection a promising path to surpassing the full history.

title: Counterfactual Rollouts for Offline Contrastive Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: Counterfactual Rollouts for Offline Contrastive Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) learns goal-conditioned values by associating state--action pairs with the states subsequently reached, assuming that no unobserved variable jointly affects the recorded action and its outcome. When offline demonstrations come from a demonstrator with information hidden from the learner, this assumption fails and the critic absorbs spurious action--outcome associations. We formalize this setting with confounded Markov decision processes and introduce counterfactual transitions that separate what the data identify from what they do not; minimizing over all compatible transitions yields a worst-case occupancy that lower-bounds the true one. Causal Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CauCRL) learns a pessimistic counterfactual transition from positive and negative offline demonstrations and trains the critic on counterfactual rollouts, substantially improving success rates over standard CRL on confounded goal-reaching tasks.

title: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
shortTitle: MCPDisCo: Seesaw-Mitigated Tuning for MCP-Native Agents
abstract: The Model Context Protocol provides a shared interaction substrate for the agentic web, allowing heterogeneous services to expose capabilities through a standardized interface. Learning to use this ecosystem entails a hierarchy of capabilities: tool-format skills, server-level transfer, and cross-server composition. We present MCPDisCo, an ecosystem-scale reinforcement learning framework for MCP-native agents. Using a Thought-Markov Decision Process (Thought-MDP), the framework explicitly represents internal reasoning alongside routing, execution, and termination and trains on real-server, long-horizon interactions spanning 70 MCP servers and 527 tools across six domains. We study the reasoning--tool seesaw, a joint-learning failure mode in which improvement in one objective can accompany deterioration in the other. To mitigate potential interference, MCPDisCo combines token-masked reward attribution with bidirectional gradient surgery: the former separates direct supervision for reasoning and action spans, while the latter removes conflicting components from both objective gradients in shared parameters. MCPDisCo achieves higher success with fewer chain-of-thought tokens. On the out-of-distribution MCP-Atlas and the GAIA benchmark, MCPDisCo maintains monotone gains, confirming that the learned behavior generalizes beyond the training server distribution and broader agentic tasks. Model weight and implementation are available.

title: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
shortTitle: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.

title: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
shortTitle: What Survives When Activation Steering Is Used as Memory
abstract: Activation steering has recently been used as a memory for skills: past experiences of an agent are stored as steering vectors and retrieved later. Facts and preferences about the user are assumed to need text instead. We test that assumption with a training-free activation memory beside a frozen LLM. The change an experience causes in late-layer states is stored as a shift, filed under a whitened key for the conversation's gist, and added back in a later session only when the gist matches. We argue that such a shift is a fixed average of an effect that attention, in context, recomputes for every question, so only question-independent content can survive. In a pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B, with judges from four model families, the memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies are unchanged), but facts are stored as the word to say, in the last layers only, and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window. Most strikingly, the reference subtracted when writing a preference decides whether its concept or its direction survives: unless the opposite is subtracted, a stored dislike is recalled as a like.

title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
shortTitle: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.
