title: Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions
shortTitle: Efficient Preconditioned Optimization Methods with Frequent Directions
abstract: Adaptive optimization methods have received considerable attention in recent years due to their strong empirical performance. However, they generally require maintaining a preconditioning matrix, which incurs prohibitive computational overhead in large-scale applications. To address these limitations, we investigate the acceleration of preconditioned optimization methods through frequent directions (FD), a widely used matrix sketching technique. We first propose FTSL by integrating FD with adaptive subgradient methods under the primal-dual framework and adding back the cumulative information discarded by FD. FTSL obtains a tighter regret bound than existing state-of-the-art results. We then apply a doubling trick that further reduces the time complexity of FTSL, while maintaining the same regret guarantee. We also consider optimization over matrix-valued decision variables and exploit their structural properties to construct sketched preconditioners. We develop FTSL-Shampoo by adapting FD to Shampoo and give a novel analysis under the primal-dual framework. To further mitigate its computational complexity, we design one-sided variants of FTSL-Shampoo under both mirror descent and primal-dual frameworks. Our algorithms not only reduce the computational cost of FTSL-Shampoo, but also achieve tighter regret bounds. We extend our methods to offline stochastic convex optimization and exploit smoothness to achieve faster convergence rates. Finally, we introduce practical variants of our algorithms and empirically demonstrate their efficiency and effectiveness across a broad range of tasks.

title: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
shortTitle: ViewStruct: View-Grounded Articulation and Connectivity Inference
abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.

title: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
shortTitle: TPPO: Tracking-Value PPO For Language Model Reasoning
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is widely used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language-model reasoning. While \emph{value evolution along trajectory} characterizes relative token-level credit, yet standard critics often fail to track it under sparse terminal rewards. To model this evolution, we analyze the relation between successive prefix values and show that they admit a Bayesian decomposition with additive updates in log-odds space. We use this additive structure to construct Tracking-Value PPO (\method), a cumulative value parameterization that sums position-wise scalar outputs into value logits. These outputs are learned through terminal-outcome supervision on the reconstructed values. \method improves aggregate mathematical reasoning scores over PPO by 7.0 and 8.4 points on Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively, while improving out-of-distribution generalization. Gains extend to Qwen3-4B, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen3.5-9B and to countdown, and scientific coding tasks. Further analysis shows more accurate tracking of value evolution and more reliable advantage estimates. Our code is publicly available in https://github.com/LINs-lab/TPPO.

title: One-Layer Transformers Provably Learn In-Context K-Nearest Neighbor Prediction with Chain-of-Thought
shortTitle: One-Layer Transformers Provably Learn In-Context K-Nearest Neighbor Prediction with Chain-of-Thought
abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enables transformers to solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate reasoning steps. Despite strong empirical success, the mechanisms by which such reasoning abilities emerge during training remain poorly understood, particularly from a theoretical perspective. In this work, we study this question in a stylized yet fully analyzable setting: in-context $\mathrm{K}$-nearest-neighbor ($\mathrm{K}$-NN) prediction with a one-layer transformer. Earlier work has demonstrated that one-layer transformers can be trained to perform $1$-NN without CoT (Li et al., 2024a) by having the softmax attention attend to the nearest neighbor in context. However, this result on $1$-NN cannot be extended to $\mathrm{K}$-NN for $K>1$, as softmax attention is much less naturally suited to attending to the 2nd through $K$-th nearest neighbors. We first give a rigorous negative result showing that this limitation already appears on a well-separated class of binary classification tasks for odd $K>1$. We then give an explicit construction of a one-layer transformer, and show that it can solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN via CoT reasoning. We further prove that, under a stylized training setup, gradient descent can recover this construction, thereby showing that transformers can acquire the capability to solve $\mathrm{K}$-NN through training. In addition, we show that the resulting trained model applies to a broader test class than that assumed in the training analysis. Our results shed light on how CoT expands the ability of transformers to learn and solve tasks that are otherwise hard to solve.

title: When Repeated Measurements Hurt Tabular Foundation Models
shortTitle: When Repeated Measurements Hurt Tabular Foundation Models
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on IID benchmarks, but how do they respond to repeated measurements at the same inputs? Across six TFMs, synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments show that additional measurements can improve predictions at measured inputs while degrading them elsewhere. Harm is most frequent at low noise, and irrelevant features amplify it in several models; real repeated-measurement datasets show similar patterns. Statistically, the IID rule targeted by PFN pretraining treats each repeated input as fresh evidence about the input distribution. When the prior links this distribution to the response function, the resulting protocol mismatch can outweigh the benefit of additional measurements, even under exact inference. Computationally, interventions identify row-count dependence in TabPFN-v3's attention scaling as a contributor to harm. Resetting the count largely reverses distortion in a noiseless linear diagnostic and attenuates amplification by irrelevant features. Finally, we evaluate ways to retain the benefits of repeated measurements while limiting their harm. Averaging measurements usually outperforms supplying them separately at larger repetition counts, whereas count reset can suppress both harm and useful gains. Code, saved results and reproduction instructions are available at https://github.com/drizmiz/PFN-Repeated-Measurement-Supp

title: Predicting Audio Popularity: A Comparative Study of Metadata and Acoustic Features Across Music and Sound Effects
shortTitle: Predicting Audio Popularity: A Comparative Study of Metadata and Acoustic Features Across Music and Sound Effects
abstract: This study addresses the prediction of audio popularity on an online sharing platform by leveraging both metadata and acoustic feature representations. Two distinct categories of audio content are considered: music and sound effects. Popularity is formulated as a supervised classification task based on two target variables: the number of downloads and the average user rating. We conduct a comparative evaluation of multiple machine learning models, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and a Neural Network model. Experiments are performed across different feature sets, including metadata, platform-provided descriptors, and eGeMAPS acoustic features. Results indicate that metadata consistently provide the most informative representation for predicting popularity. Nevertheless, acoustic features alone achieve performance significantly above chance level, demonstrating that intrinsic properties of the audio signal contribute to popularity prediction.

title: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning
shortTitle: X-Ragent: Tool-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Chest X-Ray Reasoning
abstract: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation often requires integrating visual findings with task-specific evidence rather than relying on direct visual recognition alone. While tool-augmented medical agents can supply such evidence via external modules, they often lack explicit mechanisms for learning when auxiliary evidence is needed and for preventing inapplicable quantitative evidence from entering diagnostic reasoning. To address this, we propose X-Ragent, a post-training framework for tool-augmented reinforcement learning that decouples learned auxiliary-evidence seeking from validity-gated quantitative measurement acquisition for evidence-grounded CXR reasoning. We construct Rad-CoT, a 7.7K-sample corpus combining causally ordered tool-augmented trajectories with report-style diagnostic reasoning, and use it to initialize Qwen3-VL-8B via agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We then optimize the policy with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using an accuracy-gated reward that applies process-level terms for measurement consistency and auxiliary-tool cost only to correct trajectories, preventing plausible process behavior from compensating for an incorrect diagnosis. Across three CXR benchmarks, X-Ragent achieves the strongest results, including an 8.6-point improvement on the fully held-out ChestAgentBench. By seeking evidence selectively and admitting only valid measurements, X-Ragent supports more faithful and evidence-grounded CXR reasoning.

title: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
shortTitle: Carve VFM: Carving Specialists out of Generalists, Automatic Task-Specific Compression of Vision Foundation Models
abstract: Vision foundation models (VFMs) provide transferable visual representations, but their inference cost limits deployment in many settings. Fine-tuning specializes a VFM without shrinking it; distillation shrinks it, but through expensive teacher-guided training. Structured pruning offers a more direct route by extracting a compact subnetwork from the VFM. However, as compression gets aggressive, existing methods fail because they treat subnetwork selection and recovery as separate axes. Across layers, capacity must follow task sensitivity rather than spread uniformly. Within a layer, a removal cannot be judged by importance alone; its impact also depends on how well the lost contribution can be recovered from what remains. Selection and recovery must therefore be decided jointly. We introduce Carve VFM, which resolves this interdependence. Given a VFM, a calibration set, and a parameter budget, it (i) searches for task-specific capacity allocations across layers; (ii) guides the search via an adaptive recovery-aware fitness criterion; and (iii) reconstructs removed behavior through iterative closed-form low-rank corrections merged into the surviving weights. The result is a dense encoder produced in minutes on a single GPU without backbone retraining. Across twelve benchmarks and four models from DINOv3 and MetaCLIP-2, Carve VFM achieves the highest reported mean accuracy in seven of eight backbone-budget configurations among the evaluated dense structured-pruning methods. Further fine-tuning surpasses the strongest evaluated edge model (88.1% vs. 85.8%), and carved models cut compute and memory while delivering 1.3-2.0x higher GPU throughput than the uncompressed one. These results show that the compact model you need is inside the VFM; it only has to be carved out.

title: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
shortTitle: StableJudge: A Lightweight Adversarial Defense Framework for LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to assign scalar scores that drive downstream decision-making, including tasks such as paper review and recommendation. However, LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines are vulnerable to score-hijacking prompt injection embedded in evaluated content, which corrupts scoring signals and distorts induced rankings. Existing defenses often enforce robustness by modifying the judge model itself, making safety dependent on a specific model's scale and training and requiring repeated effort when the judge is updated or replaced. We propose StableJudge, a lightweight defense framework that externalizes prompt-injection mitigation as a reusable pre-scoring capability. StableJudge centers on a compact 0.13B Sentry that localizes injected spans and performs targeted sanitization prior to evaluation, and is trained using adversarially evolving attacks to improve robustness beyond a fixed prompt set. To stabilize measurement, StableJudge derives deterministic, fine-grained scalar scores from the judge's output distribution. Across held-out scientific abstracts and out-of-distribution attack variants, StableJudge improves score recovery under attack while largely preserving general-purpose performance, demonstrating that robust LLM-based judging can be achieved by decoupling safety from judge scale via reusable defense capabilities. Code and data will be released.

title: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
shortTitle: Growing to See: Efficient Pretraining of Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
abstract: Progressive depth growth builds large networks by starting with shallow models and inserting layers during training. Recent advances in large language models have renewed interest in this longstanding approach, demonstrating benefits for training efficiency and reasoning alongside changes in internal computations. However, how growing affects representation quality and computational patterns in self-supervised vision transformers remains unclear. In this work, we systematically investigate progressive depth growth in two popular self-supervised families, namely masked autoencoders (MAE) and DINOv3, and analyze how growing affects downstream performance, intermediate representations, and internal computations. Across global and dense tasks, we show that growing improves downstream performance while reducing training FLOPs by 13.9--24.8%, with ImageNet linear-probe accuracy gains of up to 3.36 percentage points. Growing also improves downstream performance at intermediate layers and reshapes internal computational patterns, introducing recurring alternations between global and localized attention in MAE and earlier local-to-global attention progression in self-distilled DINOv3. Together, these findings establish progressive depth growth as an effective and efficient pretraining strategy for improving downstream performance across global and dense visual tasks with less computation, and advance our understanding of how growing shapes visual computation.

title: Sample-Size Extrapolation in Simulation-Based Inference via Statistical Scaling
shortTitle: Sample-Size Extrapolation in Simulation-Based Inference via Statistical Scaling
abstract: In simulation-based inference (SBI), neural posterior estimators trained on a bounded range of sample sizes can become inaccurate on larger datasets because their parameterizations do not specify how posterior location, uncertainty and shape must change as observations accumulate. We propose center-estimated NPE (CE-NPE), which combines a statistical center with an explicit contraction rate and learns a local center correction and residual densities in posterior-scale coordinates. The center is a statistical estimate, such as a closed-form statistic or a simulator-based moment match, which does not require an evaluable likelihood. Our analysis explains how contraction amplifies center error and decomposes Gaussian posterior error into shape, mean and covariance contributions. On six regular benchmarks, CE-NPE gives the best reference-posterior agreement of all tested amortized estimators at every out-of-range size, up to five times the largest training size, without retraining; it also fits better within the training range on most of them. Matched controls and nonregular examples characterize the scope of these gains and identify the conditions on which they depend: an appropriate contraction rate, an accurate center, and a stable residual representation.

title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
shortTitle: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. The key difficulty is that neural architectures are operation-labeled DAGs: edge direction defines computational flow, but existing predictors often treat direction as a local structural cue. We propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer based on encoder-wide directional consistency, which preserves directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature update. DTA-GT realizes this principle with direction- and topology-aware node initialization, Magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative sequence-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and Magnetic spectral controls show that the improvements come from coordinated direction-aware stages and edge-orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics confirm that the modules exhibit the intended directional behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.

title: Mean Accuracy Is the Wrong Estimand for a Release Decision
shortTitle: Mean Accuracy Is the Wrong Estimand for a Release Decision
abstract: A release decision about a fine-tuned model is an operational commitment about the \emph{next} rerun of its training recipe. Yet standard benchmark reporting gives only the mean accuracy of past seeds. These target fundamentally different questions: release decisions depend on catastrophic tail risk, whereas standard evaluation reports only central tendency. Because fine-tuning induces bimodal mode collapse, high average accuracy frequently conceals severe failure rates. Auditing $2\,124$ fine-tuned models across eleven language models, we show that shipping models based on mean accuracy violates a $10\%$ deployment failure budget $48.0\%$ of the time. Common heuristics like $\bar b - 2σ$ prove equally dangerous: by underestimating variance on small samples, they become most permissive when evidence is weakest. We introduce \textbf{recipe cards}, an evaluation framework that directly certifies rerun tail failure rates using exact finite-sample binomial bounds. Recipe cards reduce held-out budget violations to $0.6\%$, enforce a mathematical sample floor ($N \ge 22$) that prevents certification on thin evidence, and explicitly refuse unverified claims under domain and task shifts.

title: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
shortTitle: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
abstract: Deepfake speech detectors are typically evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions, with labels unavailable during operation. This makes it difficult to know when a detector operates in familiar conditions and can be relied on. We propose an unsupervised drift monitor that operates on the internal embeddings of a deployed detector. The monitor compares each input against bona fide and spoof references using regularized Mahalanobis distances. These distances define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the detector embedding space, allowing unfamiliar inputs to be routed for review. We evaluate the monitor on four modern detectors on three datasets. The monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage. The results also show that drift affects both classes: bona fide recordings can move away from the training reference, increasing alert rates even in in-domain settings. Our findings suggest that deployed deepfake speech detectors should be treated not only as a binary classification, but also as a reliability problem.

title: The Bell Boundary of Shared Representations
shortTitle: The Bell Boundary of Shared Representations
abstract: When does a shared representation become insufficient for jointly supporting multiple tasks? This question lies at the heart of multi-task learning models. Although task interference in shared representations has been widely observed, its onset, measurable form, and capacity boundary remain poorly understood. In this paper, we revisit this problem through the lens of Bell's theorem. We show that if four binary task outcomes can be jointly represented by a common shared representation, their correlations must satisfy the classical CHSH bound $|S|\leq2$. We introduce NCnet, a controlled multi-task model for studying how representational capacity affects task compatibility. Experiments reveal a clear capacity-dependent transition. Once nontrivial task fitting emerges, constrained capacity can yield $|S|>2$. As capacity further increases, these exceedances progressively disappear and $S$ returns to the bounded region. This systematic pattern provides evidence that limited representational capacity is an important source of the observed incompatibility. We observe similar transitions across CNNs, PLMs, and LLMs, suggesting that the phenomenon extends beyond the controlled NCnet setting. We refer to this capacity-dependent transition as the Bell Boundary, providing a measurable diagnostic for representation bottlenecks, task incompatibility, and capacity allocation in multi-task models.

title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
shortTitle: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. title: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
shortTitle: Same Operation, Different Permission: Evaluating Whether Guardrails Honor Authorization
abstract: As language-model agents write code, move money and change records on behalf of users, deciding whether an action is authorized has become a central safety problem. Guardrails are often placed in front of these actions, yet few evaluations ask whether their decisions follow authorization: blocking unauthorized actions while still allowing the same actions under valid permission. We introduce \bench{}, a benchmark that contrasts authorization evidence for the same operation in its language track. It combines expert-annotated natural-language scenarios with executed and verified operations, plus externally sourced native-policy requests. \bench{} checks each decision for correctness, usability and resulting effect, and tracks each request across guardrail changes. Our experiments show that many blocked operations stem from failed reviews, not correct denials. Repairing the output format restores usable decisions but changes which authorized requests are honored, and adding a second reviewer removes some errors while rejecting valid authorization. Guardrails should therefore be evaluated on both the unauthorized actions they stop and the authorized actions they let through.

title: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
shortTitle: Label Collapse in Diffusion Language Model In-Context Learning
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) applies large language models to new tasks by prepending a few labeled demonstrations to a query. Prior work has studied how demonstration ordering affects ICL, but the interaction between label arrangement patterns and model biases has not been systematically examined. We define label collapse as the failure mode in which the model generates query-independent labels, and show that it is architecturally universal at the tested 8-9B scale: five models spanning autoregressive (Llama-3, Qwen3.5) and discrete diffusion (LLaDA, iLLaDA, LLaDA-Instruct) families all exhibit label collapse even under the class-balanced alternating arrangement, with some label word pairs collapsing in virtually every tested condition and others flipping their collapse direction with arrangement. Critically, accuracy alone cannot detect this collapse: models can achieve near-chance accuracy while generating query-independent labels, a score indistinguishable from balanced performance, so the failure can persist undetected in deployment. We measure separation, the log-odds of the two label words at the query position (the quantity that label-bias calibration operates on), as a complementary diagnostic that exposes collapse hidden beneath surface accuracy, together with a measurement protocol that guards label extraction against tokenizer and formatting artifacts. For autoregressive models, collapse persists where the majority-label-bias account does not apply, and arrangement patterns can reverse the collapse direction; for diffusion models, we present a systematic evaluation of ICL failure modes, complementing contemporaneous studies of dLLM context comprehension and demonstration-order sensitivity, and identify open questions about how iterative denoising interacts with label biases.

title: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
shortTitle: Feature Normalization under Finite Training Budgets
abstract: Standardizing a rare feature can help stochastic gradient descent learn its effect within a finite budget, but it also changes the noise cost of learning. We characterize the lowest rare-subgroup risks attainable by standardized and unscaled training when each chooses a nonnegative constant learning rate and a deterministic stopping time under the same observation cap. For two independent binary features, we derive both optimized risks as prevalence vanishes while the expected number of rare observations remains finite. Uniform control over rates and stopping times reduces each limiting oracle to a scalar minimization. With positive noise, the preferred scaling changes exactly once as we move signal to the rare feature while the limiting risk at initialization stays fixed and positive. The formulas also explain how noise and budget affect the comparison. Separate finite-prevalence bounds favor standardization on a rare-dominant signal family and unscaled training on a common-dominant family. The results concern final iterates with population preprocessing and fresh observations. Exact-moment searches assess the approximation at finite prevalence. In a controlled study, both orderings persist under observation reuse, estimated preprocessing, and intercept fitting when tuning choices are fixed before evaluation. Selecting a predictor after observing training can reverse an ordering, even when selection uses exact population risk.

title: A Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Pose-Invariant Face Recognition and Facial Landmark Localization
shortTitle: A Multi-Task Deep Learning Framework for Pose-Invariant Face Recognition and Facial Landmark Localization

The two objectives are jointly optimized using a weighted multi-task loss, allowing the model to learn complementary semantic and spatial facial representations. The proposed framework was evaluated on the prepared CPLFW-based multi-task dataset. title: Radial Tail Repair: Post-Training Correction for Diffusion and Flow Models
shortTitle: Radial Tail Repair: Post-Training Correction for Diffusion and Flow Models
abstract: Diffusion and flow-matching models may struggle to accurately represent distributional tails, especially for heavy-tailed data. Existing approaches often use heavy-tailed noise or modify the generative dynamics, requiring dedicated retraining and more difficult estimation. We take a simpler approach: rather than relearning the full distribution, we correct only the model's behavior in the extreme regime. Our method builds on the radial-angular decomposition of multivariate heavy tails, where radius and direction become asymptotically independent. This allows us to preserve the directional structure learned by the pretrained model and correct only its radial tail. We estimate the tail onset from reference and generated samples, then rescale generated extremes so that their radial survival matches the target distribution. The resulting method is a lightweight post-training correction applied to a frozen diffusion or flow-matching model, requiring neither retraining nor changes to its sampling dynamics. Experiments on challenging synthetic heavy-tailed distributions and real weather and wildfire datasets show that this simple correction substantially improves extreme-tail coverage using only a small number of fitting samples.

title: Human-Like Redundancy Resolution for Real-Time Bimanual Humanoid Teleoperation
shortTitle: Human-Like Redundancy Resolution for Real-Time Bimanual Humanoid Teleoperation
abstract: Real-time bimanual humanoid teleoperation requires accurate wrist tracking while keeping arm configurations predictable. Because a 7-DoF arm admits multiple elbow configurations for the same wrist pose, wrist-only tracking can cause elbow drift or abrupt configuration changes. Fixed anthropomorphic constraints can stabilize elbow posture, but they can also block the redundant adjustments needed near singular configurations. We propose a human-like redundancy-resolution framework that combines adaptive elbow guidance with singularity-robust wrist tracking. Shoulder-wrist geometric retargeting generates robot-scale wrist targets. An adaptive elbow-offset criterion uses the offset direction to guide posture and scales this guidance by the offset magnitude, so the redundant degree of freedom is progressively released as the human arm straightens. A hierarchical velocity solver prioritizes wrist tracking and projects the adaptive elbow guidance into the wrist-task null space. In a fixed-wrist-target ablation, adaptive guidance reduces mean elbow-direction error by 54.4% compared with removing this guidance. In a workspace-boundary stress test, singularity-robust tracking reduces peak raw joint-velocity demand by 97.9% compared with the undamped pseudoinverse. Real-world bimanual tasks and cross-platform retargeting show applicability across robot morphologies.

title: Towards Cost-Efficient Video Dataset Construction with Large Language Models
shortTitle: Towards Cost-Efficient Video Dataset Construction with Large Language Models
abstract: Research on video classification models has witnessed significant growth recently, accompanied by a significant increase in the demand for datasets to train such models. Via a Leave-One-Rater-Out (LOO) mechanism and an Add-One-Rater-In (AORI), we evaluate the performance of the LLMs as virtual annotators. Finally, we report cost comparisons relative to existing approaches. To ensure reproducability, we made our implementation available on github.

title: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
shortTitle: ANCHOR: Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
abstract: For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one: developers also constrain how the task must be carried out-modification scope, workflow order, validation, tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of 10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations, and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10 foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches 70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14 configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting, and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.

title: Vision Models Capture Complementary Representations in Children That Converge in Adults
shortTitle: Vision Models Capture Complementary Representations in Children That Converge in Adults
abstract: How the relationship between image-text aligned and vision-only models changes across development remains unknown. We applied time-resolved representational similarity analysis to EEG data from 8-year-olds, 12-year-olds, and adults. CLIP showed significant model-brain alignment already in children, whereas vision-only models aligned more strongly later in development. Residual analyses revealed complementary structure, with CLIP retaining alignment beyond an architecture-matched vision-only model from age 8. Much of the model-brain alignment reflected semantic structure, with EEG representations of category and animacy strengthening toward adulthood, while alignment with low-level image properties remained weak across age. Together, these findings suggest that image-text aligned and vision-only models capture complementary aspects of developing visual representations and may provide useful constraints for AI systems that aim to learn and adapt over time.

title: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
shortTitle: GpFlash: Maximizing Speed and Minimizing Memory for Gaussian Process Training and Prediction
abstract:
This paper presents GpFlash, a Gaussian process library that is focused on fast training and posterior evaluations, minimal memory usage, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. GpFlash was compared to the popular GP libraries scikit-learn, GPy, GPflow, GPyTorch, and SMT on a MacBook Pro and the supercomputer Trillium. GpFlash was found to use less memory and to be faster for training and posterior evaluations relative to the other GP libraries for all cases considered. For example, when using $
x = 10^4$ training points in a 10-dimensional space GpFlash required 9.6 to 35 times less memory and was 2.6 to 54 times faster than the other GP libraries for the evaluation of the marginal log likelihood and its gradient. The memory reduction was achieved by only using one matrix of size $
x 	imes 
x$ to store different symmetric matrices in its lower and upper triangular entries. The computational speedup was the result of designing algorithms to access memory efficiently, using BLAS and LAPACK methods extensively, and factoring kernel equations so that expensive exponential calculations could be reused. GpFlash was more than 440 times faster than all of the other GP libraries considered when evaluating the posterior mean together with its gradient for the case with $10^4$ training points and 10 dimensions. GpFlash is available at https://github.com/marchildon/gpflash.

title: From Volpiano to Pixels: 30,000 Lines of OMR Ground Truth for Medieval Chant
shortTitle: From Volpiano to Pixels: 30,000 Lines of OMR Ground Truth for Medieval Chant
abstract: Optical music recognition (OMR) for medieval chant lacks training data linking manuscript images to musical symbols across notational families. Using existing Volpiano transcriptions from the Cantus Database, we created 30,567 image-target pairs from ten sources in eleven exports, including 339 verse fragments. Their target sequences contain 1,952,143 tokens. The pipeline locates staff systems, infers clefs and maps known pitches to staff positions. Six detector families handle the different layouts and notations. Where heuristics failed, two small U-Nets learned staff lines and clef letters from manual annotations. Reviews of sampled export lines found zero to four pitch or clef errors, but used different error definitions and do not provide a uniform audit of the corpus. A CRNN trained from scratch achieved a symbol error rate of 9.6 % on 3,086 test lines. The earlier model, trained mainly on Austrian sources of the 15th and 16th centuries, scored 45.3 %. In three separate training runs, each excluding one manuscript, error rates on the excluded manuscript were 21.5-31.0 %. Model-assisted alignment recovered a further 2,686 lines.

title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
shortTitle: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.

title: Davinci-Tool: Scaling Agentic Tool-Use Supervision with Verifiable Executable Environments
shortTitle: Davinci-Tool: Scaling Agentic Tool-Use Supervision with Verifiable Executable Environments
abstract: Reliable agentic tool use requires training data that pair diverse multi-step workflows with executable evidence that the requested outcomes were achieved. Scaling either trajectory coverage or verification alone is insufficient as new environments introduce distinct states, rules, and dependencies that must also be reflected in the success criteria. To address this challenge, we introduce Davinci-Tool, a 30B tool-use model, and Davinci-ToolData, an execution-grounded dataset designed to scale environment coverage and outcome verification together. Davinci-ToolData preserves restorable states, execution traces, outcomes, and verifiers as a unified substrate for supervision. Two complementary pipelines populate this substrate: Execution-Grounded Task Synthesis (EGTS) derives verified demonstrations from independently authored systems, and Executable Environment Synthesis (EES) synthesizes auditable environments, state-grounded tasks, and executable verifiers across single and coordinated domains. These pipelines yield 30,395 verified trajectories spanning 2,260 invoked tool names. We first train on these demonstrations with supervised fine-tuning, then reuse EES states and verifiers to compare alternative actions and construct outcome-grounded preferences for Direct Preference Optimization. Davinci-Tool improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 52.4 to 88.2 on $τ^2$-bench, from 30.4 to 62.8 on BFCL v4 multi-turn, and from 16.9 to 56.2 on MCP-Atlas, outperforming Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct on all three benchmarks with only 1/16 of its total parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/MassLab-SII/Davinci-Tool.

title: From Parallel to Sequential: Small-Batch Noise Restores Simplicity Bias of Muon
shortTitle: From Parallel to Sequential: Small-Batch Noise Restores Simplicity Bias of Muon
abstract: Simplicity bias, which can arise from sequential feature learning during training, has been proposed as a general explanation for the success of deep learning. An important driver of this phenomenon is saddle-to-saddle behavior, in which the gradient flow trajectory remains close to a sequence of saddle manifolds while learning one feature at a time. However, Muon, a state-of-the-art optimizer based on spectral descent, does not exhibit such dynamics in the full-batch setting and instead learns features in parallel. How is it then that Muon is so successful in deep learning settings? We show that stochastic gradient noise fundamentally changes this behavior: small-batch noise restores sequential feature learning, providing a mechanism for simplicity bias that is absent from full-batch Muon. We explain this transition through stochastic smoothing of the spectral descent operator underlying Muon. When gradients are small relative to the noise scale, the expected spectral update becomes approximately proportional to the actual gradient, which restores gradient-flow-like dynamics. We formalize this mechanism for deep linear models by deriving the effective continuous dynamics of noisy spectral descent. Experiments on low-rank matrix reconstruction, vision transformers, and large language models (LLMs) support these findings.

title: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
shortTitle: SpecGuardBench: Can Coding Agents Construct Reliable Validation Harnesses from Natural Language Specifications?
abstract: As coding agents become more capable, tests remain the primary evidence for judging whether their code is correct. Yet passing available tests does not establish that an implementation satisfies its natural language specification. Reliable validation requires checks that faithfully capture the specification and scenarios that thoroughly exercise the code, but current benchmarks provide limited insight into whether agents can construct such evidence themselves. We introduce SpecGuardBench, a benchmark of 291 tasks from 13 real-world repositories, covering 8 types of verification logic such as functional postconditions and interaction protocols. Given a natural language specification, repository context, and a reference implementation, an agent constructs a validation harness comprising executable checks and test scenarios. The checks should reject implementations that violate the specification while accepting those that satisfy it, and the scenarios should thoroughly exercise the code. Across four proprietary and open-weight coding agents, none constructs a harness scored as faithful on the benchmark's implementations for more than 63% of the tasks. The bottleneck lies less in exploring test scenarios than in constructing checks that faithfully reflect the specification. Specifically, the agents show a clear tendency to write checks that mirror the reference implementation rather than the specification, and therefore reject implementations that the specification permits.

title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
shortTitle: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC under a fixed training recipe. We find that these gains generalize across four additional evaluation settings, including the INSPIRE and eICU-CRD datasets, with improvements in macro AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 score. Our results show that simply changing how EHR data are presented to the model during pretraining can improve downstream performance, without changing the model or collecting additional data.

title: EviStress: Evidence Stress Learning for Generalizable Face Forgery Detection with Textual Explanations
shortTitle: EviStress: Evidence Stress Learning for Generalizable Face Forgery Detection with Textual Explanations
abstract: The rapid spread of face forgeries on the Web challenges the credibility of visual content. In practical Web environments, manipulated media originate from evolving generation pipelines and undergo diverse processing during dissemination, making reliable authenticity assessment under unseen manipulations and visual changes a critical challenge. We observe that a standard LoRA-adapted CLIP detector exhibits uneven patch-level decision dependence, concen trating a disproportionate share of class-specific relevance on a small fraction of visual patches. To improve robustness to variations in such highly dependent evidence, we propose EviStress, a two-stage framework for generalizable face forgery detection with textual explanations. In the first stage, Evidence-Targeted Patch Perturbation (ETPP) estimates patch dependence from global, relational, and semantic cues and assigns positively correlated perturbation probabilities, explicitly stress-testing highly dependent visual evidence during training. We further introduce Discriminative Variation Preservation (DVP), which constrains the residual between clean and perturbed representations to retain authenticity discriminative information. In the second stage, Intrinsic Evidence Instruction Tuning (IEIT) transfers the adapted CLIP encoder into LLaVA as its vision tower and performs parameter-efficient multimodal instruction tuning, enabling authenticity prediction and textual explanation directly from the learned forgery-sensitive representation without an external detector. Experiments demonstrate improved cross-dataset and cross-method generalization and corruption robustness, with the multimodal model providing authenticity predictions and human-readable explanations.

title: Acceptable Misalignment
shortTitle: Acceptable Misalignment
abstract: There is a specific challenge designers face in developing autonomous robots capable of open-ended learning. This challenge is how one can develop such systems in an ethically sound way when there are many unknowns during design time about their manner of deployment, what they can and will learn, and how these systems will act on the basis of what they have learned. One response to this challenge is to align, as far as possible, the activities and goals of autonomous robots with human values, raising the question of how to make this alignment possible, a question known as the value alignment problem. We argue that the value alignment problem faces a number of challenges that show that full alignment is both theoretically and practically impossible, meaning that misalignment incidents will keep occurring. This undermines current alignment approaches, as the attempt to maximize alignment cannot properly deal with the possibility that the risk of misalignment that remains after alignment methods have been implemented might still be unacceptable to society. To overcome this difficulty, we argue that a shift in perspective is required from a focus on the maximization of alignment to the conditions under which misalignment incidents become acceptable. In this paper, we explore what this shift in perspective entails. We introduce the concept of acceptable misalignment, formulate normative requirements for alignment mechanisms aimed at bringing misalignment incidents to an acceptable level, and we conclude by presenting a new methodological framework that consists of alignment mechanisms that can meet these requirements.

title: Learning Operators for Symmetry Discovery: From Lie Groups to Local Symmetry Geometry
shortTitle: Learning Operators for Symmetry Discovery: From Lie Groups to Local Symmetry Geometry
abstract: Continuous symmetry discovery is typically formulated as a separate estimation problem for each function or dataset. We instead investigate whether the map from a function to its symmetry structure can be learned across a family of functions from finite observations. Using the infinitesimal differential characterization of continuous symmetries, we formulate this map as an inverse symmetry operator, analogous to an inverse PDE problem. For global Lie-group symmetries, we establish a representation-theoretic population characterization: the symmetry Lie algebra is the nullspace of a positive-semidefinite operator constructed from representation coefficients and the infinitesimal group action. We also show that the inverse symmetry operator is equivariant under coordinate changes through the adjoint action. This characterization separates the geometric symmetry map from finite-sample estimation, motivating a hybrid approach that amortizes statistically difficult components while retaining analytic structure. On SO(5) benchmarks, amortized equivariant estimation of harmonic coefficients improves symmetry recovery from sparse observations, whereas ordinary least squares suffices for SL(2,R). We extend this viewpoint to local symmetries, where symmetry directions form smoothly varying tangent distributions rather than a fixed Lie algebra. Under the Lie-bracket consistency condition, Frobenius' theorem guarantees local integral submanifolds along which observables remain unchanged. We recover this geometry using a hybrid estimator that learns observation weights while preserving analytic differential and geometric recovery. Across global, non-compact, local, and physically motivated synthetic benchmarks, our results support learning the statistically difficult finite-sample components while preserving the known geometric structure of symmetry recovery.

title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
shortTitle: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).

title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
shortTitle: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

title: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers
shortTitle: Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers
abstract: Emotions are expressed on a continuum and are naturally described in the valence-arousal (VA) space. Existing VA-based image editors are typically training-based and domain-specific, limiting them to VA regions seen during training and making them brittle across datasets and domains. Meanwhile, despite producing high-quality edits, state-of-the-art foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers: non-linear emotion representations in text encoders makes prompt interpolation poorly calibrated, so accurate and continuous VA control remains unreliable. To fill this gap, we introduce Barycentric Guidance, a training-free framework that turns pretrained foundation image editors into continuous affective controllers over VA, requiring no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. Our method maps any target VA point to simplex-based guidance weights, enabling VA controllability in three aspects: (i) accurate targeting of VA states, (ii) broad coverage across the VA plane, and (iii) continuous control. Across three face datasets, we improve VA target accuracy by 25-29%, expand VA-plane coverage by 28-50%, and increase expression diversity by 29-49%, over the strongest baseline. Unlike prior domain-specific methods, our training-free approach exploits the foundation model's inherent versatility, enabling generalization beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework. Code is available at https://github.com/harveymannering/BarycentricGuidance.

title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
shortTitle: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.

title: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
shortTitle: Neural Bayesian Networks for Modular and Scalable Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
abstract: Bayesian Networks (BNs) are established tools for letting agents reason under uncertainty in sequential decision-making. They split a joint distribution into local conditional mechanisms arranged on a directed acyclic graph, which makes them modular, interpretable, and ready to perform probabilistic inference. Their classical formulation, however, has limitations in both expressiveness and scale: each conditional is usually stored as a table or a linear-Gaussian form, and inference evaluates the graph one node and one query at a time. In this paper we introduce Neural Bayesian Networks (NBNs), in which each conditional is a differentiable, tensor-valued mechanism, while the graph and its factorization are unchanged. NBNs retain the modularity and local mechanisms of BNs, can represent any learnable conditional distribution, and run natively on GPUs. We also release NBN, a PyTorch-based library for learning and inference in NBNs, together with a public benchmark. Our evaluation shows gains in both expressiveness and scale: NBNs fit distributions that classical BN libraries struggle to represent, and on large networks and large batches of queries they run two orders of magnitude faster thanks to GPU parallelization. NBN is available at https://github.com/Giovannibriglia/NeuralBayesianNetworks.

title: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
shortTitle: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.

title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
shortTitle: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.

title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
shortTitle: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
abstract: Does providing additional context to automated AI auditors improve their effectiveness? Using the Petri tool to audit LLM coding agents, we test the impact of providing two types of resources (an external codebase and benchmark transcripts) to LLM auditors, across four auditor-target LLM pairs and three behaviours (harmful compliance, reward hacking, sycophancy). (1) External codebase: We provide the auditor LLM with a fixed, external open source codebase, which prior work finds improves the realism of synthetic audits. Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout. The suppression recurs in three of four pairs under a different scenario and resource bundle. (2) External benchmark transcripts: We provide the auditor with transcripts of the target's performance on benchmarks measuring similar behaviours, intended to inform the auditor about the target's behavioural patterns. Providing this resource raises reward hacking scores in all four pairs (from 1.7 to 6.1 in one case). However, subsequent experiments show that supplying only the related benchmark's abstract, without transcripts, also increases reward hacking, and the effect is absent under a different framing of the same behaviour. Overall, we find no consistent effect of either resource outside reward hacking, but we find substantial variability in judge-scored behaviour across conditions. Our results underscore the importance of careful piloting with tools such as Petri, as the measured rate of target behaviour is highly sensitive to configuration decisions. We hope our results inspire more research into the reliability and robustness of automated alignment auditing.

title: FOCUS: A Subspecialty Foundation Model for Intraoperative Central Nervous System Pathology
shortTitle: FOCUS: A Subspecialty Foundation Model for Intraoperative Central Nervous System Pathology
abstract: Intraoperative frozen-section diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) lesions guides surgical decisions but is challenged by artefacts, diagnostic complexity and time constraints. Most pathology foundation models have limited exposure to CNS frozen tissue. Here we present FOCUS, a subspecialty foundation model pretrained on 27,930 frozen-sections enriched for CNS tissue. FOCUS led 11 internal diagnostic and 12 biomarker-prediction tasks, with mean AUCs of 0.969 and 0.877, respectively, retaining leading performance in temporal and external cohorts. To provide more comprehensive diagnostic information, we further organized ten diagnostic tasks into a WHO-aligned diagnostic hierarchy and separately evaluated FOCUS for lymphoma detection, a critical task for intraoperative surgical decision-making. In reader assessments by six neuropathologists, FOCUS assistance enabled junior readers to approach or exceed unassisted senior readers in hierarchical diagnosis and raised junior readers' lymphoma sensitivity from 81.6% to 94.7%. FOCUS could improve diagnostic accuracy and granularity, inform lymphoma-related resection decisions and provide provisional molecular information. Such capabilities highlight the potential of FOCUS to provide robust, clinically actionable support for intraoperative CNS pathology.

title: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
shortTitle: ML Engineering Agents - A Data Management Perspective
abstract: Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents are emerging as a new paradigm for automating end-to-end ML pipeline development. Using large language models for code generation and predictive performance as a machine-gradable feedback signal, these agents iteratively synthesize, execute, and refine pipeline code. Yet current systems are largely evaluated on pre-built, single-table benchmarks that abstract away key data management challenges. This tutorial introduces the foundations of MLE agents and highlights research opportunities for the database community. We cover how agents combine program synthesis with iterative and evolutionary optimization, and discuss open challenges in efficient pipeline execution, data discovery and augmentation over heterogeneous sources, reliability and debugging, as well as fairness and compliance. We connect these challenges to existing data management techniques and conclude with a hands-on session using contemporary MLE agents.

title: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
shortTitle: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window optimization methods often evaluate windows independently, overlooking temporal dependencies and potentially producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. We propose Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL), a framework that incorporates prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process for adaptive window optimization. First, TSE-RL assigns each window an explicit semantic role through Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset actions, extending binary retain/discard decisions to event-level alignment. Second, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases and promote physiologically plausible window sequences. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder captures dependencies across windows, improving training stability and computational efficiency compared with recurrent architectures. TSE-RL is plug-and-play and can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.

title: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
shortTitle: WeFair: Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in Short-Video Search
abstract: Short-video search requires compact query rewriters that infer personalized intent from brief, ambiguous queries under strict latency constraints. The challenge is to decide when personalization is warranted and generate a reformulation that preserves the user's immediate information need. A rewriter optimized for fluency or engagement may still introduce unsupported details and redirect the search toward a different intent. Existing methods often underutilize users' actual reformulations and behavioral traces, relying instead on synthetic reasoning and indirect behavioral rewards that may produce more engaging candidates but cause intent drift. To build an effective rewriter that remains faithful to user intent, we propose WeFair, Fidelity-Aware Alignment from Human Feedback for Personalized Query Rewriting in WeChat short-video search. WeFair assigns real user behavioral signals to a progression from demonstration to preference to verification. We first mine actual human reformulations from search sessions, then apply multidimensional LLM screening and contextual verification to filter unsupported transitions without extensive manual annotation. During training, we begin with a supervised curriculum that progressively builds rewriting capabilities from large-scale human personalized query demonstrations, and then use direct preference optimization to align with users' subsequent consumption. In the final on-policy optimization stage, we construct a strict verification reward based on actual human reformulations to further boost performance with group relative policy optimization. Further analysis shows that auxiliary rewards can activate more rollout groups in GRPO but reduce intent fidelity. Online A/B testing in WeChat short-video search shows a 1.576% relative increase in effective clicked-query rate (VV>10s) and a 1.731% relative reduction in query reformulation rate.

title: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
shortTitle: Estimating Uncertainty of Omnimodal Large Language Models via External Omnimodal Embeddings
abstract: Recent work has investigated Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs), models which can take multiple modalities and their combinations as input, as a way forward to have systems really capable of interacting with their environment. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for OLLMs, however, remains an open problem: existing methods largely target at most two modalities at a time, require access to model internals, or re-invocation of the evaluated model. We propose a model-agnostic UQ framework that scores a Chain-of-Thought response entirely through external omni-modal embeddings, measuring the grounding of the reasoning in the multimodal input and its internal coherence. Our contribution is the family of signals and an empirical characterisation of when it is reliable, rather than any single estimator: we find the geometric scores to be largely redundant with one another (mean within-split rank correlation 0.91-0.94) but strongly complementary to answer-dispersion baselines, and their reliability to depend on the generator and the modality. The resulting confidence estimates require no access to logits, hidden states or gradients of the evaluated model and no additional inference from it; they do require segmenting the reasoning trace with an auxiliary model and, for the aggregated score, a labelled calibration set that we show can be as small as 25 examples (although we also show that such a set buys little over fixing one signal a priori). On UNO-Bench, with both a closed and an open model, our scores yield small gains over self-consistency (systematic with the closed generator, mixed with the open one) and are competitive with self-verbalisation and internal-state baselines, especially in open-ended, omni-modal questions where previous state-of-the-art baselines struggle.

title: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
shortTitle: KNN Implementation Details Can Dramatically Change Performance: An Example from Cover Trees
abstract: Nearest neighbor search algorithms are widely used and have a long history, but we find that key implementation details are seldom reviewed in articles about them. These details can materially impact performance, and thus change the conclusions one makes about a given algorithm's superiority. In this article, we highlight these impacts by reviewing the Cover Tree as an example, producing RustKNN, a unified Rust implementation of three construction variants of the Cover Tree with three query modes. Our analysis reveals: (1) the optimal query strategy depends on $k$ and on the dataset (single-tree search is fastest at $k{=}1$ on three of our four largest datasets, while dual-tree search is fastest at $k{\ge}5$ on the three largest), and choosing the wrong query mode can cost up to a $7.5\times$ factor in runtime; (2) the cover tree base parameter, set to 2 in theory and 1.3 in practice, is not a safe default for dual-tree search: 1.3 is optimal on only one of seven datasets, and on covtype it is $1.6\times$ slower than the optimum; (3) among five micro-optimizations, only early-exit distance computation has a consistent effect, and that effect grows with dimension (none at $d{=}32$, $1.31\times$ at $d{=}54$, and $1.49\times$ at $d{=}784$); and (4) all-nearest-neighbor and held-out benchmarks yield different implementation rankings. All main timing tables report medians over 20 independent allocations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. RustKNN is open source at https://github.com/CrowdStrike/RustKNN.

title: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
shortTitle: UA-Bench: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models on Underwater Acoustic Recognition
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are fast becoming a general interface to sound, yet how far their broad pretraining carries into specialized domains remains largely open. Vessel monitoring, maritime safety, and ocean sensing all depend on recognizing underwater signals, but to our knowledge LALMs have not been systematically evaluated on them. Annotated recordings are costly to collect, and a faithful synthetic alternative has to bring together many interacting factors: the structure of detection pulses, communication waveforms, and ship-radiated noise, and the sound-speed profile, geometry, and multipath propagation through which each reaches the receiver. We address this by proposing \textbf{UA-Bench}, to our knowledge the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating LALMs on underwater acoustic signal recognition. It comprises 375,051 audio records that couple parameterized sources with modeled propagation, so that every record can be traced to the conditions that produced it. The records span these three signal families, and each carries a three-level label hierarchy (13 leaf classes), a templated multi-turn dialogue, and source and channel metadata. We evaluate on a balanced 2,600-record subset with a gated coarse-to-fine protocol that locates each error at source routing, fine-grained classification, or output format, and add a paired silent-audio control to test whether the waveform is actually used. Nine open LALMs, evaluated without task-specific adaptation, reach only 2.0\%--13.1\% leaf accuracy, against a random reference of 7.7\%. The waveform helps source routing far more than leaf recognition (for one model, +29.5 versus +2.3 points over silence), and just four models gain reliably at the leaf level, by at most 4.7 points. UA-Bench thus gives a reference point for these models, and its released training partition supports follow-up adaptation work.
